Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back, everyone. The Australian players are out in the middle. Shafali Verma and Smriti Mandhana to open for India. Ashleigh Gardner to start with the ball. Let's play...
...THE CHASE...

Aussie on verge of losing the home run - Although India initially struggled to capitalize on the new ball by conceding far too many freebies, Harmanpreet Kaur’s persistence with her seamers eventually paid off.  She kept the pace attack in the hunt. Arundhati Reddy scalped the openers' wicket. Renuka Singh Thakur removed Phoebe Litchfield cheaply while Sree Charani was in the action in the final over as she delivered a fine over, which included two run outs.  Now then, the surface remains favourable for batting, India’s disciplined recovery has transformed the contest. A victory here would be historic, marking Australia’s first T20I series loss at home in nine years.

A tale of two halves - Despite being put under tremendous pressure by a dominant 128-run opening partnership, the Indian bowlers displayed resilience to claw their way back into the contest. While Voll acted as the primary aggressor, Mooney played a steady supporting role from the other end. However, the momentum shifted decisively the moment Mooney fell, the scoring rate plummeted, and India capitalized on the opening to claim three wickets in just four overs, effectively stemming the run flow dearly and silencing the opposition’s charge.

Redemption by India! The Indian bowling unit have staged a remarkable comeback, perfectly executing the mindset that Harmanpreet Kaur demanded at the toss.  After weathering an early storm from Georgia Voll and Beth Mooney, they tightened the screws and pulled the contest back into their favor with clinical precision, giving away just 34 runs in the final five overs.

Commentary.Commentary: We are all set for the action to commence. A milestone game for Harmanpreet Kaur as she leads her troops out in her 356th international appearance. She becomes the most capped women's international cricketer across formats, going past Suzie Bates' 355 appearances. It will be the left-hand, right-hand combination of Beth Mooney and Georgia Voll to open the innings for Australia. Renuka Singh Thakur will get things going with the ball. Voll to face the first ball. A slip in place. Let's play...

India Women (Playing XI) - Smriti Mandhana, Shafali Verma, Jemimah Rodrigues, Harmanpreet Kaur (C), Richa Ghosh (WK), Deepti Sharma, Amanjot Kaur (In for Shreyanka Patil), Arundhati Reddy, Kranti Gaud, Sree Charani and Renuka Singh Thakur.

Australia Women (Unchanged Playing XI) - Beth Mooney (WK), Georgia Voll, Phoebe Litchfield, Ellyse Perry, Ashleigh Gardner, Georgia Wareham, Nicola Carey, Annabel Sutherland, Sophie Molineux (C), Kim Garth and Darcie Brown.

A bit off in Sydney, but keen to put in a response - The captain of Australia, Sophie Molineux admits they were a little off in all three departments in the previous game, but says the side is looking forward to having another crack tonight. She also confirms that Australia go in unchanged. Shares that there were a few nerves on her captaincy debut against India, but she expects tonight to feel very different.

Backing her bowlers to do the job again - The Indian skipper, Harmanpreet Kaur, feels that bowling first is a better option, looking at the conditions. Shares that their bowlers did a great job in the last game and hopes they bowl with the same mindset. On becoming the most capped player in women’s international cricket, Kaur feels it is a great achievement and is keen to continue contributing to the team.
TOSS - Sophie Molineux and Harmanpreet Kaur have made their way out for the flip of the coin. Harmanpreet calls it correctly. India elect to BOWL first.

Advantage India - As for Harmanpreet Kaur's side, they could not have asked for a better start to the series. The task now is to build on that momentum and extend their advantage in the multi-format contest. There are still areas to polish, particularly in the field, where consistency remains a work in progress for the Women in Blue. History beckons for India. Australia have not lost a T20I series at home since 2017. While this is a multi-format series, a strong performance here would mark a significant statement on Australian soil. Stick around for the toss and team news.

Action time in the capital - From Sydney, the caravan has moved to Canberra for the second of three T20Is in this multi-format series, with India holding a two-point lead after the opening game. For Australia, it was a case of batters getting starts but no one going on to make a defining contribution. What stood out was the intent, as every batter who walked in looked to play their shots. Expect that aggressive approach to continue, though perhaps with more responsibility.
... MATCH DAY ...

Second act in Canberra - It wasn’t the cleanest start for the highly anticipated series between Australia and India Down Under, with rain playing spoilsport in the opener. India still edged it via DLS, but it felt like a game half-told. Now, from Sydney to the capital city of Canberra, the tour moves on with the second T20I ready to pick up the pace with the Women in Blue leading 1-0. These two sides will take the field at the famous Manuka Oval only after 2020. A massive gulf - India may have won the last round, but zoom out, and it’s Australia running the show at 26-9. India have only cracked three wins in the last ten, one of those coming in a nerve-shredding Super Over in 2022. Down Under, though, the script tightens a bit, with Australia just 7-5 ahead, close enough to keep the rivalry nicely on edge. The cutting edge in bowling - The Indian bowlers stole the show at the Sydney Cricket Ground, skittling Australia out for a below-par 133 with two overs still in hand, a rare sight on their own turf. Riding the rhythm from the recently concluded WPL, the attack has looked sharp, in sync, and a step ahead. Arundhati’s four-for and Renuka’s 2 for 14, including a maiden, showed just how well they’ve hit the ground running. The real test now is holding that edge and sustaining the momentum. India didn’t get much batting time in the opener, but they’ll still count on Mandhana and Shafali to lay the platform. The real weight, though, sits with Harmanpreet Kaur and Smriti Mandhana, the two pillars of India’s batting against Australia in T20s. Between them, they’ve stacked up 12 fifties, five for Harmanpreet and seven for Mandhana, and more often than not, when these two click, India dominate. I don’t think it was a false start - Words from Australian coach Shelley Nitschke after the defeat in the series opener, where rain played a key role as well. However, it sure was an underwhelming performance with the bat by Australia. Then again, stepping into the shortest format after nearly a year can bring a touch of rust. The flip side in today’s fast-evolving women’s T20 landscape is simple, momentum is everything. And Australia will know they need to find it quickly with the World Cup looming mid-year. The firepower is still very much there. Beth Mooney, Australia’s leading run-scorer against India with 913 runs at an average of 43.47 and nine fifties, remains a constant threat. Add to that a lineup stacked with depth and all-round options right down to number nine, and there’s no shortage of experience. The only bit of concern? Ellyse Perry’s form with the bat. Plenty of starts, plenty of 20s and 30s, but no half-century since 2023. And with bigger stages approaching, she’ll be itching to turn those starts into something substantial. Team form (Last 5 T20Is, latest first) AUSTRALIA - LWWWW | INDIA - WWWWW. What to expect? With the points-based system in play, the outcome will hinge on who accumulates the most points across all three formats. Australia will draw confidence from their win over India at Manuka Oval in 2020 and will look to replicate a similar performance in the Sophie Molineux era. Let’s hope that the rain stays away and we get a full game of cricket this time around between two quality teams.
